paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised quantum machine learning for fraud detection

summary: The paper evaluates quantum kernel methods for credit‑card fraud detection using IQP feature maps with data re‑uploading (d=3) on simulated quantum circuits up to 20 qubits. On a 500‑sample Kaggle dataset (25 fraud cases), the quantum kernel SVM achieves up to ~15 percentage‑point higher average precision than classical RBF kernels in both supervised and one‑class anomaly detection tasks. All results are obtained via noiseless statevector simulation on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.

experiments.description: Supervised fraud classification using quantum kernels with an IQP-style feature map and data re-uploading, compared against classical logistic regression and RBF SVC baselines.

algorithm.variant: quantum kernel classification with IQP feature map and data re-uploading

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One feature per qubit; 28 anonymized credit-card features are reduced by PCA to N principal components, with N matched to the qubit count.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary fraud classification via kernel SVM maximizing average precision on labeled fraud vs genuine transactions.

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud detection on a Kaggle dataset of anonymized transactions.

dataset_specification.description: Subsampled to 525 total samples including 25 fraud cases; only the 28 anonymized features are used; PCA applied to retain the first N principal components.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Standard scaling feature-wise; PCA dimensionality reduction; features scaled by eta=0.1 before quantum embedding; t-SNE used for visualization.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision (AP) versus number of features/qubits; compared against classical baselines.

hardware.provider: NVIDIA A100 GPU (classical HPC for statevector simulation)

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Standard scaling and PCA; hyperparameter tuning by random search for classical baselines.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average precision computed from predicted scores; Gram matrices assembled from quantum kernel evaluations.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical one-class SVM with RBF kernel
speedup_claims.conditions: unsupervised fraud detection on the subsampled Kaggle credit-card dataset with PCA preprocessing and IQP feature map re-uploaded d=3
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a performance advantage in average precision, not a computational speedup; results are from statevector simulation, not hardware.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical RBF kernels for supervised fraud classification
speedup_claims.conditions: for feature counts above about 10 qubits/features
speedup_claims.caveats: Reported for supervised classification; no asymptotic advantage proven.
Same scaling is stated for both quantum and classical kernel methods; no quantum speedup claimed.
This is a cost statement, not a speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Kernel evaluation requires O(N_s^2) Gram-matrix evaluations for training and O(N_d N_s) for inference.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical kernel methods also require O(N_s^2) Gram-matrix evaluations; the paper discusses this as the baseline scaling.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Around 10-20 features/qubits in the reported experiments; no asymptotic crossover proven.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Empirical performance gap appears around 10–20 qubits/features but only on a 500‑sample toy dataset.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Authors suggest ≥50–100 qubits and deeper kernels would be needed to reach regimes not simulable classically.
limiting_factors: Only statevector simulation; no real quantum hardware evaluation
Problem size extremely small (500 samples, ≤20 qubits)
No asymptotic speedup or complexity advantage proven
Kernel Gram matrix still requires O(Ns^2) evaluations like classical SVM
Quantum kernel evaluation fully classically simulable at tested sizes

notes: Hardware type inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states statevector simulation and GPU execution, with no real QPU used.
Circuit depth not explicitly reported; d=3 re-uploadings and IQP layers are described, but total depth is not given.
Paper reports a ~10–15% average precision improvement over classical RBF kernels at 20 qubits but only in simulation and on a small dataset.
No theoretical runtime speedup over classical methods is claimed or demonstrated.

experiments.description: Unsupervised fraud anomaly detection using quantum kernels inside one-class SVM, compared against classical RBF OC-SVM.

algorithm.variant: quantum kernel one-class SVM with IQP feature map and data re-uploading

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One feature per qubit; PCA-reduced features are embedded into an N-qubit register.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Novelty detection / anomaly detection by separating nominal transactions from anomalies using a one-class SVM in quantum feature space.

problem_instance.description: Unsupervised credit-card fraud detection on a subsampled Kaggle dataset.

dataset_specification.description: 525 samples total with 25 fraud cases; only nominal data used to train OC-SVM; evaluation uses labels only for AP scoring.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Feature-wise standard scaling; PCA to N principal components; features scaled by eta=0.1 for quantum embedding.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision versus number of features/qubits; nominal-only training for OC-SVM; labels used only for AP evaluation.

hardware.provider: NVIDIA A100 GPU (classical HPC for statevector simulation)

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Standard scaling, PCA, and hyperparameter tuning for classical baselines.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average precision computed from anomaly scores; Gram matrices built from quantum kernel overlaps.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical one-class SVM with RBF kernel
speedup_claims.conditions: unsupervised anomaly detection on the subsampled Kaggle credit-card dataset with PCA preprocessing and IQP feature map re-uploaded d=3
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a metric improvement, not a runtime speedup; results are from statevector simulation on GPU.

speedup_claims.factor: O(N_s^2) kernel evaluations for training; O(N_d N_s) for inference
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper discusses scalability limits and does not demonstrate a computational speedup.

speedup_claims.factor: weeks to months training time for large datasets; real-time inference only if single-entry test is sub-millisecond
speedup_claims.conditions: future quantum hardware and large industrial datasets
speedup_claims.caveats: These are hardware-time estimates, not measured experimental results.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Training requires O(N_s^2) kernel evaluations; inference requires O(N_d N_s) kernel evaluations.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical OC-SVM with RBF kernels also requires O(N_s^2) Gram-matrix evaluations.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Reported separation begins past about 10 features and reaches about 15% AP advantage at 20 qubits; no asymptotic crossover proven.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Performance separation reported after ~10 qubits, reaching ~15% AP advantage at 20 qubits.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Authors speculate that ≥50–100 qubits and faster kernel evaluation hardware would be required to move beyond classical simulation limits.
limiting_factors: Experiment performed entirely with noiseless statevector simulation
Dataset reduced to 500 samples to enable simulation

No runtime speedup over classical OC‑SVM
Kernel circuits remain classically simulable at tested qubit counts

notes: Hardware type inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper explicitly says statevector simulation on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.
Circuit depth not explicitly reported; only the re-uploading count d=3 and IQP structure are given.
Paper reports unsupervised anomaly detection AP reaching ~0.7 at 20 qubits vs ~0.55 for classical RBF OC‑SVM (~15% gain).
